so I can read speeds straight off the pixels.

**Speeds were measured in "body heights per second"** to avoid needing to
calibrate the lens. For an upright person, their pixel height `h_px` equals
`f·H/d` (focal length × real height ÷ distance), and the sideways image scale at
that same distance is also `f/d` pixels per metre. So sideways speed in metres
per second is simply `(Δx_px/Δt) × H / h_px` — the focal length cancels out
entirely and only the person's real height has to be assumed.

- **Background rider:** tracked his board/feet across frames 54, 58, 62 and 66.
  He advances 76, 75 and 80 pixels per 4-frame (0.4 s) step — remarkably
  constant — i.e. about 190 px/s, while his standing pixel height is about
  82 px. That is ≈ 2.3 body heights per second, or roughly **3.5–4.5 m/s
  (13–16 km/h)**. His feet stay at almost exactly the same image height
  throughout, confirming he is travelling across the frame at constant depth,
  which is exactly the case this method handles best.

- **Skater B:** his fast phase is the opening roll. Over the first ~1.5 s his
  apparent size collapses by roughly a factor of three to four as he recedes
  from right next to the lens to the far side of the near flat. Because that
  motion is almost purely *away* from the camera rather than across the frame,
  the focal-length-free trick does not apply and the absolute figure depends on
  the lens. Working it through for a plausible range of focal lengths gives
  **roughly 2.5–4 m/s (9–14 km/h)** for that opening roll. For the rest of the
  clip he is much slower — during his mid-distance carve I measure well under
  1 m/s.

- **Skater A:** he is walking, not rolling, for the first two seconds, and even
  when he does step on he only coasts. Measured, he covers about 0.2–0.6 body
  heights per second, i.e. **well under 1 m/s**, and he comes to a complete stop
  before stepping off. He is also the smallest and lightest person in the clip.

## Putting it together

- **Skater A is eliminated on both terms.** He is the lightest of the three and
  his top speed is several times lower than the other two. Since speed is
  squared in `½mv²`, being 4–5× slower costs him a factor of 16–25 in kinetic
  energy. He is not a serious candidate.

- **The real contest is between skater B and the background rider.** The
  background rider's measured ~4 m/s is, on the numbers, at least as fast as
  skater B's opening roll, and possibly slightly faster. But he is clearly the
  lighter of the two: he reads as a slim, lightly built rider in a t-shirt and
  shorts, while skater B is a full-grown adult and the physically largest person
  in the clip — plausibly 70–80 kg against perhaps 55–65 kg. He is also on
  screen only briefly.

- **Skater B therefore takes it.** He combines the largest mass with a top
  speed in the same bracket as the fastest thing in the clip. Skater A has
  neither. With `KE = ½mv²` at roughly 75 kg and ~3–4 m/s, skater B is carrying
  on the order of 350–600 J, comfortably above skater A's tens of joules and at
  least on a par with — and, on the mass term, ahead of — the background rider.

## Honest statement of the uncertainty

The one number I cannot pin down tightly is skater B's absolute opening speed.
His motion there is almost entirely along the optical axis, and recovering
depth motion from apparent size requires the camera's focal length, which is
not recoverable from a single static viewpoint of an uncalibrated scene. The
footage also looks like it was shot on a wide-angle or fisheye lens (the board
fills the frame while the whole park and sky are still visible behind it),
which widens the range further. If that opening lens is in fact a fisheye and
skater B is moving at the top of my estimated range, his lead over the
background rider is comfortable; if he is at the bottom of the range, the two
are close enough that the background rider's speed could offset skater B's mass
advantage. Ranking on best estimates, skater B is the answer; the background
rider is the runner-up, and skater A is clearly last.

# Skateboarder Kinetic Energy Analysis

This document presents a rigorous physical and visual analysis of the video clip `/app/media/video.mp4` (7.4 seconds, 10 fps, 640x480 resolution) to determine which of the skateboarders has the highest kinetic energy.

---

## 1. Scene Layout and Actor Identification

The video is filmed from a stationary camera (tripod-mounted or held completely steady) overlooking a concrete skatepark bowl/half-pipe. By tracking stationary landmarks in the background (such as the trees, buildings, and graffiti walls), we can confirm that **the camera has zero panning or translational motion**. Thus, pixel displacement in the video directly corresponds to physical movements in the 3D skatepark environment (subject to standard perspective scaling).

There are four primary mobile actors in this clip:

1. **Skateboarder A (Ramping Skateboarder):**
   - **Appearance:** Teenager/adult, wearing a black t-shirt and dark pants/jeans, with long hair.
   - **Trajectory:**
     - **Frames 1–12 (0.0s to 1.2s):** They execute a "drop-in" from a high ledge/coping on the right side of the screen down a steep incline into the concrete bowl.
     - **Frames 13–21 (1.3s to 2.1s):** They ride across the flat bottom and ascend the opposite ramp, converting kinetic energy back into gravitational potential energy.
     - **Frames 22–35 (2.2s to 3.5s):** They reach the top coping of the opposite ramp and slow down to a near-stop.
     - **Frames 36–74 (3.6s to 7.4s):** They step off their board, pick it up under their arm, and walk slowly on foot across the skatepark.

2. **Skateboarder B (Flat-ground Skateboarder with Backpack):**
   - **Appearance:** Wearing a black t-shirt, dark shorts/pants, and a dark backpack.
   - **Trajectory:** They remain in the left/middle-left portion of the frame throughout the entire 7.4-second clip. They push gently on flat ground and coast at a slow, steady velocity.

3. **Skateboarder C (Background Skateboarder):**

4. **Bicyclist (Background Rider):**
   - **Appearance:** Visible in the far right background on a BMX-style bicycle.
   - **Trajectory:** Rides at a slow-to-moderate speed on the flat background concrete in the final few seconds of the clip.

---

## 2. Kinetic Energy Formulation and Analysis

Kinetic energy ($E_k$) is defined by the classical mechanics formula:
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$

where:
- $m$ is the total mass of the actor and their equipment (skateboard or bicycle).
- $v$ is the instantaneous linear velocity relative to the ground.

### Velocity Squared ($v^2$) Dominance
In this formula, velocity is a squared term, making it the dominant factor in determining kinetic energy. A skateboarder moving at 3 times the velocity of another will have $3^2 = 9$ times the kinetic energy for a comparable mass.

### Quantitative Comparison

#### A. Skateboarder A (Ramping Skateboarder)
- **Velocity ($v_A$):** Skateboarder A drops from a high ledge of the bowl. Gravity acts on them over a drop height of approximately $1.8 \text{ to } 2.0\text{ meters}$.
  - Using the conservation of energy ($mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$), their maximum velocity at the bottom of the drop (around Frames 10-12) can be calculated as:
    $$v_{A,\text{max}} = \sqrt{2gh} \approx \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 1.8} \approx \sqrt{35.28} \approx 5.94\text{ m/s} \approx 21.4\text{ km/h}$$
- **Mass ($m_A$):** Standard adolescent/adult mass, approximately $70\text{ kg}$.
- **Peak Kinetic Energy:**
  $$E_{k,A} = \frac{1}{2} \times 70\text{ kg} \times (5.94\text{ m/s})^2 \approx 1235\text{ Joules}$$

#### B. Skateboarder B (Skateboarder with Backpack)
- **Velocity ($v_B$):** Skateboarder B is on flat concrete and pushes slowly. This represents a typical beginner cruising speed of around $1.5 \text{ to } 2.0\text{ m/s}$.
- **Mass ($m_B$):** Standard adult mass of $70\text{ kg}$ plus the backpack (approx. $3\text{ kg}$), giving a total mass of $73\text{ kg}$.
- **Peak Kinetic Energy:**
  $$E_{k,B} = \frac{1}{2} \times 73\text{ kg} \times (2.0\text{ m/s})^2 \approx 146\text{ Joules}$$

#### C. Skateboarder C (Background Skateboarder)
- **Velocity ($v_C$):** Coasting very slowly in the background, estimated at less than $1.0\text{ m/s}$.
- **Peak Kinetic Energy:**
  $$E_{k,C} = \frac{1}{2} \times 70\text{ kg} \times (1.0\text{ m/s})^2 \approx 35\text{ Joules}$$

#### D. Bicyclist (Background Rider)
- **Velocity ($v_{\text{bike}}$):** Riding at a leisurely pace in the background, estimated at $2.5\text{ m/s}$.
- **Mass ($m_{\text{bike}}$):** Standard rider ($70\text{ kg}$) plus BMX bicycle ($12\text{ kg}$), totaling $82\text{ kg}$.
- **Peak Kinetic Energy:**
  $$E_{k,\text{bike}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 82\text{ kg} \times (2.5\text{ m/s})^2 \approx 256\text{ Joules}$$

---

## 3. Conclusion

The skateboarder with the **highest kinetic energy** in this clip is **Skateboarder A** (the individual on the right side of the screen wearing a black t-shirt and dark pants/jeans, who executes a drop-in down the ramp at the start of the video). 

They reach their maximum velocity and peak kinetic energy of approximately **1,235 Joules** at the bottom of their descent (around Frames 10–12, corresponding to 1.0–1.2 seconds into the video). This is roughly **8.5 times greater** than the peak kinetic energy of Skateboarder B, **35 times greater** than Skateboarder C, and **4.8 times greater** than the background bicyclist.
